newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer - US has potential to keep up strong dlr.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer - US has potential to keep up strong dlr.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer on Thursday said he believed the U.S. has the economic potential and the credibility to maintain a strong dollar as well, as the political will to do so.

"It is gratifying for the international community to recognise that today the United States has not only the economic potential and the credibility to maintain a strong dollar but also the political will to do so," Tietmeyer said.

Tietmeyer said in the text of a speech to The Economic Club of New York that markets have become more sensitive to any potential change in the stance of a country's monetary and fiscal policy and that credibility was critical.
He said credibility has become a vital asset for banks, helping to lower interest rates and also market volatility.
But he said in the speech, which was released in Frankfurt under embargo, that the ability of central banks to influence market trends has waned.
"A country's credibility depends not only on its monetary policy but also on its economic and fiscal policy stance," Tietmeyer said.
"And it is only credibility on both these counts that helps to keep volatility at bay, such as exchange rate volatility," he said, welcoming the U.S. commitment to a strong dollar.

Tietmeyer said credibility was a prerequisite for any successful monetary policy and that it must also be the criterion for assessing any proposal of closer international cooperation on macroeconomic policy.
"There is no point in 'leaning against the wind' in exchange markets," Tietmeyer said. "The objectives of international cooperation must therefore be realistic."
He said that some situations may indeed make sense for coordinated joint action, for example in foreign exchange markets but that these were only "specific situations".
But Tietmeyer, citing the problems in the European exchange rate system in the early 1990s, noted the impact was limited and that "markets love to probe into fixed exchange rates".
"Under present-day conditions, however, international cooperation for the sake of influencing market trends makes little sense, and has little prospect of success," he said.
"In the normal case, policy makers can influence markets only very indirectly, namely by means of adequate and credible domestic policies," Tietmeyer said.
Tietmeyer also reiterated that government bail-outs of banks "pose moral hazard problems" and that central banks, including the IMF, must be only a lender of last resort.
"Central banks should make clear that they are only the lender of last resort to ensure the provision of adequate liquidity for the banking system of their respective country as a whole," he said.
He said banks should "never be put in the awkward position" of being a lender of first resort for a bank in trouble.
He said that present-day financial markets "have not become more vulnerable all around" and that changes have been made to make the financial system more robust.
